content: Chronic pain is a common issue for individuals with spinal cord injury (SCI). Traditionally, this pain is managed with medications, but long-term use of these drugs often proves ineffective and is associated with significant side effects. Non-pharmacological treatments are frequently recommended as alternatives, but their benefits and risks remain unclear due to methodological limitations in existing research. The objective of this review was to critically evaluate and synthesize the available evidence on the effects of non-pharmacological interventions for managing chronic neuropathic and nociceptive pain in individuals with SCI. A comprehensive search of multiple databases and clinical trial registries was conducted, with the initial search completed in March 2011 and an update performed in November 2014. However, the results of the updated search have not yet been incorporated into the analysis. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated non-pharmacological interventions for chronic pain in SCI patients. A total of 16 trials involving 616 participants were identified. These studies examined eight different types of interventions, including electrical brain stimulation (transcranial direct current stimulation [tDCS] and cranial electrotherapy stimulation [CES] in five trials, and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation [rTMS] in three trials), exercise programs (three trials), acupuncture (two trials), self-hypnosis (one trial), transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) (one trial), and a cognitive behavioral program (one trial). None of the included trials were deemed to have a low overall risk of bias. Twelve studies were classified as having a high risk of bias, while the risk of bias in four studies was unclear. The overall quality of the evidence was weak, with significant methodological flaws such as inappropriate selection of control groups undermining the validity of the findings. For tDCS, pooled data showed a reduction in pain scores on an 11-point visual analogue scale (VAS) of -1.90 points (95% confidence interval [CI] -3.48 to -0.33; P = 0.02) in the short term and -1.87 points (95% CI -3.30 to -0.45; P = 0.01) in the mid-term. Exercise programs demonstrated the largest treatment effects, with reductions in chronic shoulder pain of -1.9 points on the Short Form-36 (SF-36) pain item (95% CI -3.4 to -0.4; P = 0.01) and -2.8 points on the pain VAS (95% CI -3.77 to -1.83; P < 0.00001). However, interventions such as rTMS, CES, acupuncture, self-hypnosis, TENS, and cognitive behavioral programs did not provide evidence of significant pain reduction. Ten trials assessed outcomes beyond pain, including anxiety, depression, and quality of life, but the data were too limited to draw definitive conclusions. Four trials reported no side effects, while five trials noted mild and transient side effects. There was no evidence of serious or long-lasting adverse effects associated with the interventions. In conclusion, the current evidence is insufficient to support the effectiveness of non-pharmacological treatments for reducing chronic pain in individuals with SCI. Further research is needed, particularly well-designed RCTs with adequate sample sizes, to better understand the benefits and risks of these commonly used interventions.
